explanation: Jesus broke bread and shared wine, saying 'This is my body' and 'This is my blood of the new covenant.'

stem: In which garden did Jesus pray in deep anguish before his betrayal, sweating drops like blood?
explanation: Jesus prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane: 'Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me; yet not my will, but yours be done.'

stem: For how many pieces of silver did Judas Iscariot betray Jesus to the chief priests?
explanation: Judas agreed to deliver Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, fulfilling prophecy.

stem: How many times did Peter deny knowing Jesus before the rooster crowed twice?
explanation: Peter denied Jesus three times in the courtyard of the High Priest Caiaphas.

stem: Which Roman governor sentenced Jesus to crucifixion despite declaring him innocent three times?
explanation: Pontius Pilate washed his hands in front of the crowd and delivered Jesus to be crucified.

stem: What criminal was released by Pilate instead of Jesus according to the crowd's demand?
explanation: The crowd stirred by the chief priests demanded the release of Barabbas the insurrectionist.

stem: Who was compelled by the Roman soldiers to carry Jesus' cross on the road to Golgotha?
explanation: Simon of Cyrene, an African from modern Libya, was compelled to carry the cross.

stem: What were Jesus' final words on the cross as recorded in John's Gospel?
options: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'
'Into your hands I commit my spirit'
explanation: In John 19:30, after receiving the sour wine, Jesus said 'It is finished', bowed his head and gave up his spirit.

stem: Who provided his own new rock-cut tomb for Jesus' burial?
explanation: Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy council member, asked Pilate for Jesus' body and laid it in his new tomb.

stem: On which day following his crucifixion did Jesus rise victoriously from the dead?
explanation: Jesus rose early on the first day of the week (the third day according to the Scriptures).

stem: Who was the first person to encounter the risen Christ outside the empty tomb on Easter morning?
explanation: Mary Magdalene saw the risen Jesus near the tomb and was sent to tell the apostles.

stem: Which apostle doubted Jesus' bodily resurrection until he saw and touched the nail prints in his hands?
explanation: Thomas declared he would not believe unless he placed his fingers into the wounds; Jesus appeared and Thomas confessed 'My Lord and my God!'

stem: Before ascending to heaven, what mandate did Jesus give his disciples in the Great Commission?
options: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them
Remain forever in Jerusalem under Roman law
Construct grand cathedrals in every village
Seek political office in the Sanhedrin
explanation: Matthew 28:19-20 records the Great Commission to disciple all nations.

stem: On which Jewish festival was the Holy Spirit poured out upon the disciples with tongues of fire in Jerusalem?
explanation: Acts 2 describes the Holy Spirit falling on the Day of Pentecost with sounds like a violent wind and tongues of fire.

stem: How many souls were converted and added to the church after Peter's first sermon on Pentecost?
explanation: Acts 2:41 records that about three thousand souls received his word and were baptized.

stem: At which gate of the Jerusalem Temple did Peter and John heal the man lame from birth?
explanation: Peter said: 'Silver or gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.'

stem: Which husband and wife died suddenly in the presence of Peter after lying about the sale price of their land?
explanation: Acts 5 records the swift divine judgment upon Ananias and Sapphira for lying to the Holy Spirit.

stem: Who was the first Christian martyr stoned to death while praying for his executioners' forgiveness?
explanation: Stephen, one of the seven deacons, was stoned outside the city while seeing the heavens opened (Acts 7).

stem: On the road to which city did Saul encounter the blinding light of the risen Christ?
explanation: Saul was traveling to Damascus to arrest Christians when Jesus spoke to him: 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?'

stem: Which Roman centurion in Caesarea was directed by an angel to send for Peter, marking the Gentile pentecost?
explanation: Cornelius was a God-fearing Gentile whose household received the Holy Spirit as Peter preached (Acts 10).

stem: In which city were the disciples of Jesus first called 'Christians'?
explanation: Acts 11:26 states that the disciples were called Christians first at Antioch.

stem: Which king executed James the brother of John with the sword and imprisoned Peter?
explanation: Herod Agrippa I killed James and arrested Peter during the feast of Unleavened Bread (Acts 12).

stem: How was Peter miraculously delivered from prison on the eve of his public trial?
options: An angel of the Lord appeared, loosened his chains, and opened the iron gate
An earthquake destroyed the city walls
The guards were bribed by the disciples
explanation: An angel struck Peter on the side, woke him, and led him past two guard posts and out through the iron gate.

stem: Who accompanied Saul (Paul) on his first missionary journey commissioned by the Holy Spirit at Antioch?
explanation: Barnabas and Saul set out from Antioch, taking John Mark with them as an assistant (Acts 13).

stem: What major doctrinal controversy was resolved at the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15?
options: Whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and obey the whole Mosaic law
Which Gospels should be included in the canon
Whether Christians should pay taxes to Caesar
explanation: The Council decreed that Gentile converts did not need to be circumcised to be saved by grace.

stem: In Philippi, why were Paul and Silas thrown into prison during their second missionary journey?
options: Paul cast out a spirit of divination from a slave girl whose owners profited from fortune-telling
They refused to worship the statue of Caesar
explanation: The slave girl's owners dragged Paul and Silas to the magistrates when their hope of making money was gone.

stem: What happened at midnight while Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns in the Philippian dungeon?
options: A violent earthquake shook the foundations, opened all doors, and loosed everyone's bonds
An angel carried them away invisibly
explanation: The miraculous earthquake caused the Roman jailer and his entire household to believe and be baptized (Acts 16).

stem: At Athens, where did Paul deliver his famous philosophical address concerning the altar 'To an Unknown God'?
explanation: Paul spoke at the Areopagus about the Creator God who does not live in temples built by human hands (Acts 17).

stem: According to Romans 3:23, what is the universal spiritual condition of humanity?
options: 'All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God'
explanation: Paul teaches universal human fallenness and the necessity of justification by faith in Christ.

stem: In Romans 6:23, what are the wages of sin contrasted with?
options: The free gift of God which is eternal life in Christ Jesus
explanation: Paul states: 'For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.'

stem: In 1 Corinthians 13, which theological virtue is declared to be the greatest, enduring forever?
explanation: Paul concludes: 'And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.'

stem: According to Galatians 5:22-23, which of the following is an aspect of the Fruit of the Spirit?
options: Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control
Accumulation of worldly riches and titles
explanation: Paul lists the ninefold fruit produced by the Holy Spirit in the believer's life.

stem: In Ephesians 6, what represents the defensive piece of armour that extinguishes all the flaming arrows of the evil one?
explanation: Ephesians 6:16 specifies the shield of faith to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked one.

stem: In Philippians 4:6, what does Paul instruct believers to do instead of being anxious about anything?
options: In every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God
Rely entirely on horoscopes and omens
Retreat completely from society into isolation
Compel others to solve all personal problems
explanation: Paul provides the biblical antidote to anxiety: prayer, thanksgiving, and God's peace.

stem: According to Colossians 3:23, whatever work a Christian undertakes should be done:
options: With all heart, as working for the Lord and not for human masters
Only when the supervisor is actively watching
explanation: Believers are instructed to view all honest vocation as service rendered directly to Christ.

stem: In 1 Timothy 6:10, what is identified as the root of all kinds of evil?
explanation: Scripture warns that the obsessive love of money leads people away from faith into many griefs.

stem: According to James 2:26, what is faith without good works compared to?
options: A body without the spirit, which is dead
explanation: James argues that authentic saving faith is evidenced by active deeds of righteousness.

stem: In 1 John 4:8, what foundational characteristic of God's nature is revealed?
explanation: The Apostle John writes: 'Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.'

stem: In Romans 13:1-7, what is the Christian's ethical responsibility toward governing civil authorities?
options: Be subject to governing authorities as servants appointed by God to maintain justice and pay taxes
Overthrow civil government by violent revolt
Disregard all civic laws and public taxes
explanation: Paul instructs Christians to submit to legitimate state authority, obey laws, and pay taxes faithfully.

stem: According to Christian marital ethics in Ephesians 5, husbands are commanded to love their wives just as:
options: Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her
explanation: Husbands are called to emulate Christ's self-sacrificing, nurturing love for the Church.

stem: In which cave did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) receive the very first divine revelation of the Holy Qur'an?
explanation: The Prophet received the first five verses of Surah al-Alaq in the Cave of Hira on Mount Nur.

stem: Which angel was sent by Allah to convey divine revelations to the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)?
explanation: Jibril (Gabriel) is the Angel of Revelation in Islam.

stem: What is the first Arabic word revealed to the Prophet Muhammad in Surah al-Alaq?
explanation: Surah 96 begins with 'Iqra' bismi Rabbika alladhi khalaq' (Read in the name of your Lord).

stem: How many chapters (Surahs) are there in the standard compilation of the Holy Qur'an?
explanation: The Holy Qur'an contains exactly 114 Surahs.

stem: Which Surah of the Qur'an is known as 'Umm al-Kitab' (Mother of the Book) and recited in every Raka'ah of Salat?
explanation: Surah Al-Fatihah is recited in every unit of prayer.

stem: Which is the longest Surah in the Holy Qur'an?
explanation: Surah Al-Baqarah (The Cow) contains 286 verses and is the longest chapter.

stem: Which verse in Surah Al-Baqarah is known as the 'Verse of the Throne', renowned for Allah's supreme sovereignty?
explanation: Ayat al-Kursi describes Allah's eternal living nature and total dominion.

stem: Which short Surah is considered equivalent to one-third of the Qur'an in theological reward due to its pure declaration of Tawhid?
explanation: Surah Al-Ikhlas declares Allah's absolute oneness and eternal, unbegotten nature.

stem: Together, Surah Al-Falaq and Surah An-Nas are known as:
explanation: They seek Allah's protection from evil and whispered temptations.

stem: Which Surah was revealed to reassure Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) when revelations temporarily ceased?
explanation: Surah Ad-Duha was revealed with 'Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor is He displeased.'

stem: Surah Al-Fil commemorates the miraculous defeat of Abraha and his army of elephants attacking:
explanation: Surah Al-Fil recounts how Allah destroyed the army with flocks of birds casting baked stones.

stem: Which Caliph ordered the definitive compilation of the standardized Qur'anic text sent to all Muslim provinces?
explanation: Caliph Uthman unified the Mus-haf based on the Quraishi dialect.

stem: Who was the chief scribe appointed to lead the official committee compiling the Qur'an?
explanation: Zayd ibn Thabit had memorized the entire Qur'an and served as the primary scribe.

stem: What are the Surahs revealed before the Prophet's migration (Hijrah) to Madinah called?
explanation: Surahs revealed prior to the Hijrah are classified as Makkan (focusing primarily on Tawhid and faith).

stem: Which night during Ramadan is celebrated as the night the Qur'an was sent down from the Preserved Tablet?
explanation: Surah Al-Qadr describes Laylat al-Qadr as better than a thousand months.

stem: In Surah Al-Ma'un, who is condemned for ostentatious prayer and denying assistance?
options: Those who pray only to be seen and refuse basic small acts of kindness
Those who give charity in public
explanation: Surah Al-Ma'un denounces hypocritical display and neglect of orphans and needy.

stem: What does the term 'Tafsir' mean in Islamic studies?
options: Exegesis and detailed interpretation of the Qur'an
explanation: Tafsir refers to the systematic theological and linguistic explanation of Qur'anic verses.

stem: What are the rules governing the proper pronunciation and phonetics of Qur'anic recitation called?
explanation: Tajweed designates the phonetic rules for pronouncing every Arabic letter correctly during recitation.

stem: Which Surah begins without the Bismillah ('In the name of Allah, Most Gracious, Most Merciful')?
explanation: Surah At-Tawbah is the only chapter in the Qur'an that does not open with the Basmalah.

stem: In which Surah does the Bismillah appear twice (at the beginning and in verse 30)?
explanation: Surah An-Naml contains Bismillah in verse 30 inside Prophet Sulaiman's letter to Queen Bilqis.

stem: What does the Arabic term 'Hadith' specifically refer to in Islamic scholarship?
options: The recorded sayings, deeds, and tacit approvals of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)
explanation: Hadith denotes the narrations recording the statements, actions, and approvals of the Prophet.

stem: The chain of narrators transmitting a Hadith from generation to generation is termed the:
explanation: Isnad is the unbroken transmission chain of narrators back to the Prophet or Companion.

stem: The actual text or body content of a Hadith narration is known as the:
explanation: Matn refers to the substantive spoken words or description in the Hadith.

stem: A Hadith categorized as possessing an unbroken chain of upright, reliable narrators is classified as:
explanation: A Sahih Hadith meets all stringent criteria of reliability and continuous transmission.

stem: Which famous 9th-century scholar compiled the celebrated collection 'Sahih al-Bukhari'?
explanation: Imam Al-Bukhari compiled the most authoritative canonical collection of Sahih traditions.

stem: Together, Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are reverently referred to in scholarship as:
explanation: As-Sahihayn denote the two foremost authoritative collections of prophetic Hadith.

stem: According to the famous Hadith of Umar, 'Actions are judged by...'
explanation: The Prophet stated: 'Innamal a'malu bin-niyyat' (Actions are judged by intentions).

stem: What is a Hadith Qudsi?
options: A sacred narration where the Prophet narrates words revealed by Allah not part of the Qur'an
A Hadith about the city of Jerusalem
A narration composed by the Caliphs
A Hadith with only two narrators
explanation: Hadith Qudsi contains divine meanings expressed in the Prophet's phrasing.

stem: Which compilation of forty fundamental ethical traditions was prepared by Imam Yahya an-Nawawi?
explanation: An-Nawawi's Forty Hadith covers the core pillars and ethical foundations of Islam.

stem: In Hadith ethics, what does the Prophet say about anyone who 'believes in Allah and the Last Day'?
options: 'Let him speak good or remain silent'
explanation: The Prophet taught restraint in speech as a mark of true faith in Allah and the Last Day.

stem: Which Companion of the Prophet narrated the largest number of Hadith traditions?
explanation: Abu Hurairah narrated over 5,300 traditions due to his constant companionship and memory.

stem: Which wife of the Prophet was a prolific scholar and transmitted more than 2,000 Hadith narrations?
explanation: Aisha (RA) was renowned for her deep jurisprudence, memory, and religious teaching.

stem: What is a 'Da'if' Hadith?
options: A weak narration lacking one or more conditions of authenticity in chain or narrator reliability
A narration recited only in secret
explanation: A Da'if Hadith suffers from a discontinuity in chain or weakness in a transmitter's accuracy.

stem: What does 'Sunnah' encompass in Islamic life?
options: The exemplary life pattern, normative customs, and model practice of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH)
Only the voluntary prayers at night
The legal codes of Ottoman rulers
explanation: Sunnah represents the Prophet's comprehensive practical living model for Muslims.

stem: According to the Prophet, which person is considered truly strong?
options: The one who controls his temper when angry
The one who overpowers others in wrestling
The one who accumulates the most wealth
The one who runs the fastest
explanation: The Prophet taught: 'The strong man is not the one who can wrestle; rather, the strong man is the one who controls himself in a fit of rage.'

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q36
stem: What is the core Islamic doctrine of the absolute, indivisible oneness of Allah called?
explanation: Tawhid is the supreme foundation of Islamic theology and monotheism.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q37
stem: What is the gravest, unforgivable sin in Islam if one dies without repenting?
explanation: Associating partners or deities with Allah is strictly condemned as Shirk.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q38
stem: Which of the following is an attribute belonging exclusively to Allah (Al-Khaliq)?
options: The Creator of all things out of nothing
Subject to birth and physical death
explanation: Al-Khaliq means the supreme Originator and Creator of all existence.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q39
stem: How many beautiful names and attributes of Allah (Asma'ul Husna) are traditionally emphasized in Hadith?
explanation: The Prophet stated that Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever enumerates and lives by them enters Jannah.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q40
stem: Which angel is entrusted with blowing the Trumpet (Sur) to inaugurate the Day of Resurrection?
explanation: Israfil will sound the trumpet twice: first causing all to fall unconscious, second raising all to life.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q41
stem: Which angels are tasked with recording all good and bad human deeds on a person's shoulders?
explanation: Kiraman Katibin record every spoken word and action.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q42
stem: Which angels question the deceased soul in the grave regarding their Lord, religion, and Prophet?
explanation: Munkar and Nakir conduct the questioning in the Barzakh (intermediate realm).

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q43
stem: Which heavenly scripture was revealed to Prophet Musa (Moses)?
explanation: Islam teaches that Allah revealed the Tawrat to Musa.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q44
stem: Which scripture was bestowed upon Prophet Dawud (David)?
explanation: The Zabur was given to Prophet Dawud (David).

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q45
stem: Which scripture was revealed to Prophet Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus)?
explanation: The original Injil was revealed to Isa (Jesus) as guidance and light.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q46
stem: Who is recognized in Islam as 'Khatam an-Nabiyyin' (The Seal and Final of the Prophets)?
explanation: Qur'an 33:40 affirms Muhammad as the Seal of all divine Prophets.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q47
stem: What does the fifth Article of Faith, 'Yawm al-Qiyamah', refer to?
options: The Day of Resurrection and Final Judgment
The start of the lunar month
The day of communal Friday prayer
explanation: Yawm al-Qiyamah is the Day of Judgment when all will account for their deeds before Allah.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q48
stem: What is the concept of divine pre-ordainment and Allah's absolute decree known as?
explanation: Qadar is belief in Allah's timeless divine knowledge, will, creation, and decree.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q49
stem: What is the state of human existence between physical death and the Day of Resurrection called?
explanation: Barzakh is the intermediate barrier realm where the soul resides until the resurrection.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Articles of Faith Q50
stem: What does 'Ihsan' mean according to the Hadith of Jibril?
options: To worship Allah as if you see Him, for though you see Him not, He certainly sees you
To give away all personal clothing
To perform Hajj every single year
explanation: Ihsan is spiritual excellence and heightened God-consciousness in all worship.

stem: What is the first pillar of Islam that declares faith in Allah's oneness and Muhammad's prophethood?
explanation: The Shahadah is: 'Ash-hadu an la ilaha illallah, wa ash-hadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah.'

stem: How many obligatory daily prayers (Fard Salat) must a Muslim perform?
explanation: The five prescribed daily prayers are Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib, and Isha.

stem: The ritual minor ablution with water required before performing Salat is called:
explanation: Wudu involves washing face, hands to elbows, wiping head, and washing feet to ankles.

stem: When water is unavailable or medically harmful, what symbolic dry purification using clean earth is permitted?
explanation: Tayammum is dry purification using clean sand or earth in place of water.

stem: The major full-body ritual bath required after major ritual impurity is known as:
explanation: Ghusl is the complete washing of the entire body with clean water.

stem: What is the direction towards the Ka'aba in Makkah faced by Muslims during prayer called?
explanation: Muslims throughout the world turn to face the Qiblah (the Ka'aba in Makkah) in prayer.

stem: The call to obligatory prayer proclaimed from the mosque is known as the:
explanation: The Adhan summons the faithful to the congregation for prayer.

stem: Which weekly communal prayer replaces Dhuhr on Friday afternoons with a Khutbah (sermon)?
explanation: Jumu'ah is the mandatory Friday congregational service featuring two sermons and two Raka'ahs.

stem: What is the funeral prayer performed for a deceased Muslim called?
explanation: Salat al-Janazah is a collective communal obligation (Fard Kifayah) without prostrations.

stem: What is the minimum wealth threshold a Muslim must possess for one full lunar year before Zakat becomes due?
explanation: Nisab is the qualifying wealth benchmark (equivalent to gold or silver value) for Zakat.

stem: What is the standard annual rate of Zakat payable on qualifying cash savings and trade merchandise?
explanation: The established Zakat rate on liquid wealth and savings exceeding the Nisab is 2.5%.

stem: During which Islamic lunar month is the obligatory dawn-to-sunset fast (Sawm) observed?
explanation: Sawm during the blessed month of Ramadan is the fourth pillar of Islam.

stem: What is the pre-dawn meal consumed before beginning the daily fast called?
explanation: Suhoor is the blessed meal eaten prior to the break of dawn before initiating the fast.

stem: What is the evening meal that breaks the fast at sunset called?
explanation: Iftar is the meal eaten immediately after sunset at Maghrib to end the daily fast.

stem: What special charitable donation (Zakat al-Fitr) must be paid before the Eid al-Fitr prayer?
options: Food grain or its equivalent given so the poor may celebrate Eid
A gold coin to the government
explanation: Zakat al-Fitr purifies the faster and ensures the needy have sustenance on Eid day.

stem: In which Islamic lunar month does the annual pilgrimage of Hajj take place?
explanation: Hajj rituals are performed between the 8th and 12th of Dhul-Hijjah in Makkah.

stem: The sacred state of consecration and simple white unstitched garments worn by pilgrims during Hajj is:
explanation: Ihram signifies spiritual equality, purity, and detachment from worldly distinctions.

stem: What is the circumambulation of the Ka'aba seven times counter-clockwise called?
explanation: Tawaf consists of walking around the Ka'aba seven times beginning at the Black Stone.

stem: The rapid walking seven times between the two hills of Safa and Marwah commemorates the desperate search for water by:
explanation: Sa'i reenacts Hajar's search for water for her infant son Ismail before Zamzam sprang forth.

stem: The pivotal, indispensable standing ritual of Hajj performed on the plain of Mount Mercy is at:
explanation: The Prophet declared: 'Al-Hajju Arafah' (Hajj is Arafat); missing Wuquf invalidates Hajj.

stem: In what year was Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) born in the Year of the Elephant?
explanation: The Prophet was born in Makkah around 570 CE during the Year of the Elephant.

stem: Who was the mother of Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) who passed away when he was six years old?
explanation: Aminah bint Wahb passed away at Abwa when Muhammad was six years of age.

stem: Which Bedouin foster mother nursed young Muhammad in the desert of Banu Sa'd?
explanation: Halimah cared for the Prophet during his early childhood years in the desert.

stem: Before receiving prophethood, by what honorable titles was Muhammad widely known among the Quraish?
explanation: The Makkans revered his impeccable integrity and honesty with these titles.

stem: Who was the wealthy Makkan merchant noblewoman who became the Prophet's first wife and first convert to Islam?
explanation: Khadijah (RA) comforted and supported the Prophet when the first revelation descended.

stem: To which African Christian kingdom did the early persecuted Muslims migrate for sanctuary under King Negus (Najashi)?
explanation: The Prophet advised his companions to seek refuge in Abyssinia where a righteous king ruled.

stem: The year 619 CE in which both Khadijah and Abu Talib passed away is historically known as:
explanation: The Prophet mourned the loss of his beloved wife and his protective uncle in the same year.

stem: The miraculous nocturnal journey of the Prophet from Makkah to Jerusalem and ascent through the seven heavens is called:
explanation: Al-Isra was the night journey to Al-Aqsa, and Al-Mi'raj was the heavenly ascension.

stem: In 622 CE, the historic migration of the Prophet and his companions from Makkah to Yathrib (Madinah) is termed:
explanation: The Hijrah marks the inception of the Islamic lunar calendar (1 AH).

stem: What were the native Muslim helpers of Madinah who welcomed and shared their homes with the Makkan emigrants called?
explanation: The Ansar received the Muhajirun in unprecedented fraternal solidarity and brotherhood.

stem: What was the first major defensive battle in Islamic history fought on the 17th of Ramadan in 2 AH?
explanation: At Badr, 313 Muslims overcame a heavily armed Makkan force of about 1,000.

stem: In 628 CE, what pivotal peace treaty was signed between the Muslims and the Quraish establishing a ten-year truce?
explanation: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah paved the way for massive peaceful expansion and the opening of Makkah.

stem: In 8 AH (630 CE), how did the Prophet Muhammad enter Makkah during its conquest (Fath Makkah)?
options: Humbly bowing on his camel and granting general amnesty to his former persecutors
Demanding revenge and execution of all leaders
explanation: The Prophet showed historic clemency, declaring: 'Go, for you are free!'

stem: During his Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada') on Mount Arafat, what did the Prophet proclaim regarding racial equality?
options: An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, except by piety (Taqwa)
The Quraish are superior to all human beings
explanation: The Farewell Sermon laid the timeless foundation of human brotherhood and anti-racism.

stem: Who was chosen by consensus as the first Rightly Guided Caliph (Khalifah) after the death of the Prophet?
explanation: Abu Bakr was unanimously appointed at Saqifah as the first successor to the Prophet.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rightly Guided Caliphs Q86
stem: Which Caliph was given the honorific title 'Al-Faruq' (The Discriminator between Truth and Falsehood)?
explanation: Umar was renowned for his justice, firmness in truth, and administrative wisdom.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rightly Guided Caliphs Q87
stem: Which Caliph was known as 'Dhun-Nurayn' (Possessor of the Two Lights) because he married two daughters of the Prophet?
explanation: Uthman married Ruqayyah and, after her death, Umm Kulthum.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rightly Guided Caliphs Q88
stem: Which cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet was the fourth Rightly Guided Caliph, renowned for supreme valor and eloquence?
explanation: Ali was celebrated for his profound spiritual depth, bravery, and legal judgments.

stem: In Islamic jurisprudence (Usul al-Fiqh), what are the four primary sources of Shariah law in proper order?
options: Qur'an, Sunnah, Ijma' (Consensus), and Qiyas (Analogical Reasoning)
Qur'an, Roman Law, Custom, and Philosophy
Hadith, Royal Decrees, Opinions, and Dreams
Tafsir, Arabic Grammar, Poetry, and Fables
explanation: Classical Islamic jurisprudence establishes the Qur'an and Sunnah as primary, followed by Ijma' and Qiyas.

stem: Actions that are strictly prohibited and punishable under Islamic law are classified as:
explanation: Haram designates unlawful acts whose performance incurs sin and punishment.

stem: Actions that are recommended and rewardable, but whose omission is not sinful, are termed:
explanation: Mustahabb acts are virtuous and praised without incurring blame if left undone.

stem: The payment or receipt of usury, interest, and unjustified excess in commercial transactions is forbidden under the term:
explanation: Riba is unequivocally forbidden in the Qur'an and Sunnah to protect economic equity.

stem: What does the ethical concept of 'Birr al-Walidayn' command all Muslims to practice?
options: Filial piety, utmost benevolence, and obedience to parents
explanation: Honouring and treating parents with kindness is paired directly with worshipping Allah alone.

stem: What is the Islamic legal marriage contract between a man and woman based on mutual consent called?
explanation: Nikah is the sacred, lawful marital agreement requiring offer, acceptance, witnesses, and Mahr.

stem: What mandatory bridal gift is given by the groom to the bride as her exclusive property upon marriage?
explanation: Mahr is the lawful gift given directly to the bride as her sole economic entitlement.

stem: What is the waiting period observed by a divorced or widowed woman before remarriage called?
explanation: Iddah ensures lineage clarity and allows reconciliation in revocable divorces.

stem: In Islamic inheritance law (Mirath), what share is fixed for a sole surviving daughter if there are no sons?
explanation: Surah An-Nisa 4:11 specifies half the estate for a single daughter in the absence of male heirs.

stem: What is a permanent religious endowment or trust dedicated for public welfare or religious purposes called?
explanation: Waqf is an irrevocable charitable endowment providing hospitals, water wells, and schools.

stem: What does the Quranic moral instruction 'Amr bil-Ma'ruf wa Nahy 'an al-Munkar' mandate?
options: Enjoining what is good and forbidding what is wrong
explanation: Enjoining good and reproving wrong is a foundational collective obligation in Islam.

stem: What is the comprehensive Islamic virtue of God-consciousness, moral piety, and reverence for Allah called?
explanation: Taqwa is the inner spiritual shield and moral vigilance against disobeying Allah.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q1
stem: In Akan traditional theology, what does the divine name 'Onyankopon' signify?
options: The Almighty God who alone is great and supreme
The god of fertility and rain
The spirit of the ancestral elders
explanation: Onyankopon conveys the absolute greatness and supremacy of the one Creator God.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q2
stem: What does the Akan appellation 'Tweduampong' literally translate to in traditional religion?
options: The dependable tree upon which one leans without falling
explanation: Tweduampong conveys God's unshakeable dependability and sustaining providence.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q3
stem: Among the Ewe people of Ghana and Togo, what is the Supreme Being called?
explanation: Mawu is the transcendent Supreme Creator in Ewe indigenous religion.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q4
stem: In Ga traditional religion, what is the sacred name for the Supreme God?
explanation: Ataa Naa Nyonmo signifies God as both fatherly protector and motherly provider of rain and life.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q5
stem: Among the Yoruba of West Africa, what is the name of the Supreme Being?
explanation: Olodumare is the supreme ruler of heaven and the cosmos in Yoruba belief.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q6
stem: Why are there generally no physical temples or images built for the Supreme Being in West African traditional religion?
options: Because God is omnipresent, infinite, and cannot be circumscribed or depicted by human hands
Because people fear God will become angry
Because indigenous people lacked building materials
Because traditional religion forbids community gatherings
explanation: African theology holds that God is too immense and omnipresent to be contained in physical structures.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q7
stem: What is the traditional Akan symbol 'Gye Nyame' (Except God) associated with?
options: The omnipotence, supremacy, and immortality of God alone
The power of chiefs over commoners
The bravery of hunters in the forest
explanation: Gye Nyame expresses that nothing exists or happens without the will and power of God.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q8
stem: In indigenous cosmology, what is the role of the Supreme Being in relation to the universe?
options: He is the Originator, Architect, and Sustainer of the cosmos
A created being who emerged from the ocean
A minor deity subservient to nature spirits
An ancestor elevated to high office
explanation: Traditional religion universally regards the Supreme Being as the uncreated First Cause.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q9
stem: What does the traditional myth of God's withdrawal to the distant sky explain?
options: The transition from intimate primordial communion caused by human triviality to the use of intermediaries
The creation of the sun and moon
The migration of ethnic clans across rivers
explanation: The myth (such as an old woman pounding fufu hitting God's sky) illustrates human disruption of divine proximity.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q10
stem: How do devotees predominantly communicate with the Supreme Being in daily life?
options: Through spontaneous short prayers, proverbs, and via subordinate deities and ancestors
Only by traveling to an ocean sanctuary
Never, because God is completely unapproachable
explanation: Devotees utter spontaneous ejaculatory prayers to Nyame while employing intermediaries in formal rites.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q11
stem: What does the Akan name 'Odomankoma' emphasize about the nature of God?
options: The Bountiful, Gracious, and Infinite Creator who continually provides
The god of war and victory
The spirit dwelling in tall trees
explanation: Odomankoma signifies the abundant grace and infinite, unending creative power of God.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q12
stem: In Dagbon (Northern Ghana), what is the traditional title for the Supreme God?
explanation: Naawuni is the Almighty God worshipped by the Dagomba people.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q13
stem: Among the Tallensi of Upper East Ghana, which term designates the High God and heaven?
explanation: Na'ayin is the celestial supreme deity associated with destiny and life breath.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q14
stem: What moral attribute is universally ascribed to the Supreme Being in traditional religion?
options: Impartial justice, absolute holiness, and love for truth
explanation: God is believed to be the ultimate sanctioner of morality and ethical righteousness.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q15
stem: What is the 'Nyame Dua' (God's tree/altar) traditionally placed in Akan family compounds?
options: A three-forked branch holding a clay basin or pot for offerings and rainwater consecrated to God
A carved wooden totem of an animal
A boundary stone marking family land
explanation: Nyame Dua is a household shrine dedicated exclusively to the Supreme Being for domestic veneration.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q16
stem: What is the symbolic meaning of rain in West African traditional cosmology?
options: A tangible blessing, life-giving fertility, and mercy poured down by the Supreme Being
explanation: Rain is celebrated as heaven's seed fertilizing Mother Earth (Asaase Yaa) to produce harvest.

stem: In Akan traditional religion, what is the sacred earth goddess revered as the custodian of fertility and burial called?
explanation: Asaase Yaa is Mother Earth, respected on Thursdays and acknowledged before tilling or digging graves.

stem: Why are no animal sacrifices or libations offered to the earth on Thursdays in Ashanti traditions?
options: Thursday is observed as the sacred rest day of Asaase Yaa
It is reserved exclusively for warfare
Animals cannot walk on farms on Thursday
The rivers dry up on Thursdays
explanation: Thursday is sacred to Asaase Yaa; tilling the soil is prohibited to honor the earth's rest.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q19
stem: In traditional thought, how does the Supreme Being reward good moral deeds and punish wicked actions?
options: Through blessings of peace, health, progeny, or misfortune, illness, and untimely death
By casting souls into physical lakes of sulfur
By giving paper certificates in dreams
He ignores all human moral behavior
explanation: Retribution and blessing in ATR are experienced primarily in earthly lineage well-being and generational continuity.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Concept of God Q20
stem: Which of the following proverbs encapsulates the belief that God is universally known to all people?
options: 'Obi nkyere abofra Nyame' (No one points out God to a child)
'The mouth that eats does not talk'
'A crab does not give birth to a bird'
'When the cat goes away the mice play'
explanation: This classic Akan maxim indicates that knowledge of God's existence is intuitive and universal.

stem: What are the lesser deities and divinities called in Akan indigenous religion?
explanation: Abosom are the subordinate nature deities functioning as ministers and children of Nyame.

stem: What is the collective name for traditional tutelary spirits and divinities among the Ga people?
explanation: Jemawonji are the nature spirits and territorial divinities revered in Ga state religion.

stem: In traditional theology, what is the ontological relationship between the Supreme Being and the divinities?
options: The divinities are created agents, messengers, and intermediaries of the Supreme Being
The divinities created the Supreme Being
The divinities are equal rivals to God
The Supreme Being is unaware of the divinities
explanation: Divinities derive all their delegated authority and vital force directly from Onyankopon.

stem: Which famous sacred river in Ghana is personified as one of the most prominent Akan national deities?
explanation: Ta Kora (the deity of the Tano River) is the prime son of Nyame and a revered national tutelary spirit.

stem: What are the nature spirits believed to inhabit deep forests, rivers, and wilderness known as in Akan folklore?
explanation: Mmoatia are believed to possess herbal wisdom and inhabit dense virgin groves.

stem: In Ewe indigenous religion, what are the departmental divinities and spiritual forces termed?
explanation: Trowo are the protective deities acting as intermediaries between humans and Mawu.

stem: What are personal or tutelary deities established to protect individual families and clans called?
explanation: Family deities protect lineage members from malevolent forces and curses.

stem: What is the primary spiritual danger of relying on malevolent spirits (sorcery or witchcraft / bayie)?
options: It destroys human life, sows division, and violates cosmic moral order
It makes a person too wealthy
explanation: Witchcraft (bayie) is viewed as anti-social malice used to cause sickness, barrenness, and misfortune.

stem: What material objects are commonly consecrated as focal dwelling points or shrines for deities?
options: Specially prepared brass pans, river stones, consecrated pots, and carved wooden stools
explanation: A consecrated brass basin containing herbs, river mud, and sacred ingredients serves as an abosom shrine.

stem: How does a person become a traditional priest or priestess (Okomfo)?
options: Through spirit possession, ancestral calling, and intensive apprenticeship under a senior priest
By buying a certificate in town
By inheriting it automatically regardless of desire
explanation: Divine calling usually manifests through possession fits followed by years of rigorous shrine training.

stem: What color of cloth and talcum powder do traditional priests and priestesses typically wear during ministrations?
options: White calico cloth and white clay (hyire)
explanation: White calico and white clay symbolize ritual purity, sanctification, and spiritual victory.

stem: What is the traditional bell or rattle used by priests to invoke spirits and rhythmic trances called?
explanation: The dawuru and gourd rattles provide the rhythmic cadence that invites spiritual possession.

stem: What is the role of the traditional herbalist (Dunsinini) in Ghanaian communities?
options: Healing physical and spiritual ailments using botanical knowledge, barks, roots, and prayers
explanation: The herbalist combines extensive indigenous pharmacology with spiritual diagnosis and healing.

stem: What is divination (abisa / afa) in traditional religion primarily used for?
options: To diagnose the spiritual causes behind mysterious sicknesses, misfortunes, and determine remedies
explanation: Divination uncovers hidden spiritual disharmony, unfulfilled vows, or ancestral displeasure.

stem: In Ewe and Yoruba cultures, what is the celebrated system of geomantic divination called?
explanation: Afa / Ifa is an intricate mathematical divination corpus using sacred palm nuts and poetic verses.

stem: What are the living-dead or ancestors called in Akan indigenous culture?
explanation: Nsamanfo are the departed forebears who live on in the spiritual realm (Asamando).

stem: Where are the ancestral spirits believed to dwell after physical death?
explanation: Asamando is the spiritual abode where righteous ancestors continue their existence.

stem: Which of the following is an indispensable condition for a deceased person to become an ancestor?
options: Living a morally upright life, attaining ripe old age, and leaving good progeny and reputation
Dying in a tragic vehicle crash while young
explanation: Ancestorship requires moral integrity, natural old age, parenthood, and an honorable death.

stem: What kind of death disqualifies a person from being admitted into the ancestral fold?
options: 'Bad death' (otoofo) such as suicide, leprosy, murder, or dying in childbirth
Dying peacefully at age 90 in one's sleep
explanation: Violent, shameful, or taboo deaths are deemed cursed, preventing communion in Asamando.

stem: What sacred rite is performed to invite, honor, and communicate with God and the ancestors using alcoholic drinks or water?
explanation: Libation involves pouring liquid on the ground accompanied by spoken prayers to God, deities, and ancestors.

stem: In what physical royal object are the collective souls and spirits of deceased chiefs preserved?
explanation: Consecrated black stools serve as the spiritual altars of departed rulers and kings.

stem: What is the biennial or six-weekly Akan festival where the Black Stools are fed and venerated in the stool house?
explanation: Adae festivals are sacred days of remembrance when chiefs offer meat, mashed yam, and libation to royal ancestors.

stem: Why are the ancestors considered vital guardians of the living family community?
options: They act as moral watchdogs, protect lineage purity, and mediate blessings from the Supreme Being
They return to claim all family money
They live as ghosts to terrify people
explanation: Ancestors are the invisible elders who uphold family morality, prosperity, and peace.

stem: What is the traditional food of the spirits prepared from mashed yam and palm oil offered during festivals?
explanation: Eto (mashed yam with palm oil, garnished with boiled eggs) is the sacred food offered to spirits and celebrants.

stem: Why is a drop of water or drink symbolically spilled on the ground before a traditional elder drinks?
options: To offer the first sip in respect to the ancestors dwelling beneath
To test if the drink is poisonous
explanation: This universal daily gesture acknowledges that the ancestors share in the community's sustenance.

stem: What is the role of the chief (Ohene) in relation to the ancestral stool?
options: He is the living custodian, mediator, and representative of the ancestral founders on the throne
He is the sole owner who can sell the stool
He is higher than all ancestors combined
explanation: The chief holds the stool in sacred trust and must rule according to ancestral customs.

stem: In Akan society, what happens if an installed chief breaks a major ancestral taboo or abuses power?
options: He is destooled (removed from the royal stool) through customary trial
He is given a lifetime pension
explanation: Destoolment enforces accountability and purifies the sacred office from disgrace.

stem: What is the female co-ruler who selects the candidate for chieftaincy and represents the matrilineal ancestors called?
explanation: The Queen Mother is the mother of the clan, possessing deep knowledge of royal genealogy.

stem: What is the royal spokesman and diplomat who conveys the chief's words and holds the staff of office called?
explanation: The Okyeame is the master orator, custodian of proverbs, and official royal mouthpiece.

stem: What happens to an ancestor if the living family members forget to offer them remembrance and libation?
options: The ancestor is believed to fade into distant obscurity and withhold familial blessings
The ancestor turns into a beast
Nothing, it has no traditional meaning
explanation: Ancestral presence depends on mutual reciprocity: the living remember them, and they protect the living.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q51
stem: What is the traditional naming and outdooring ceremony of a newborn baby among the Akan called?
explanation: Dintoo is the ceremony on the eighth day when the baby is given an identity and presented to the world.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q52
stem: Among the Ga people, what is the infant outdooring and naming rite called?
explanation: Kpodziemo takes place at dawn on the eighth day to introduce the child to the community and elements.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q53
stem: Why is a child not given a formal name and kept strictly indoors until the eighth day after birth?
options: To ensure the baby has come to stay as a true human rather than an ephemeral spirit visitor (kosanba)
To allow the baby to learn how to speak
explanation: The child is observed for seven days to confirm stability before being recognized as a full human being.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q54
stem: During the Akan naming ceremony, what symbolic substances are placed on the baby's tongue with the words 'When you say water, let it be water'?
explanation: This moral ritual instructs the child to speak the uncompromised truth throughout life.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q55
stem: What is the famous puberty initiation rite for adolescent girls among the Krobo and Dangme people called?
explanation: Dipo initiates young Krobo maidens into responsible adulthood, chastity, and civic motherhood.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q56
stem: What is the puberty rite of passage for girls among the Akan called?
explanation: Bragoro celebrates a young woman's first menstruation, preparing her for honorable marriage.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q57
stem: What was the traditional customary penalty for a girl who became pregnant before undergoing her puberty rite (Kyirbra)?
options: Severe social ostracism, heavy ritual pacification fines, and banishment into the village outskirts
She was made queen of the town
explanation: Kyirbra (pre-puberty pregnancy) was regarded as an abomination that polluted the land and ancestors.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q58
stem: What values are inculcated into young women during indigenous puberty rites?
options: Personal hygiene, domestic management, fidelity, infant care, and moral self-respect
explanation: Puberty rites serve as traditional finishing schools preparing maidens for noble womanhood.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q59
stem: In West African traditional marriage, what is the 'Knocking Fee' (Kokooko / Abowmu bodze)?
options: The customary presentation of drinks and cash by the groom's family to formally declare marital intention
The money paid to rent the wedding hall
A fee paid to the police
explanation: The knocking rite seeks formal permission from the bride's parents to initiate marital negotiations.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q60
stem: Why is traditional marriage viewed as a covenant between two whole families and lineages rather than just two individuals?
options: Because it unites clans, ensures mutual support, lineage continuation, and collective social responsibility
Because the bride has no say in her marriage
To allow the family to take all the groom's property
Because the law requires sixty witnesses
explanation: Traditional marriage cements enduring alliances between extended ancestral kin groups.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q61
stem: What constitutes the customary bride wealth (Tiri Nsa / Dowry) in traditional Ghanaian marriage?
options: Specified customary drinks, cloths, money, and gifts presented to the bride's parents and clan
A written treaty signed in parliament
explanation: Tiri Nsa legalizes the union, legitimizes offspring, and compensates the bride's maternal family.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q62
stem: Under what circumstances could a traditional marriage be customarily dissolved (divorce)?
options: Proven chronic adultery, barrenness, witchcraft, infectious incurable disease, or extreme neglect
A minor quarrel over cooking salt
The husband losing a board game
The wife buying a new dress
explanation: Divorce requires exhaustive customary family arbitration and only occurs under severe irreconcilable conditions.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q63
stem: Why are elaborate funeral celebrations staged in Ghanaian indigenous societies?
options: To ensure a peaceful and dignified transition of the soul into Asamando to join the noble ancestors
To show off family wealth and entertain tourists
Because traditional religion requires dancing every week
explanation: Proper burial and funeral rites allow the spirit to cross the threshold into the ancestral realm.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q64
stem: What is the widowhood rite (Kuna) traditionally performed for a surviving spouse?
options: Rites of ritual cleansing, severance of matrimonial bonds, and protection from the deceased spouse's ghost
Forcing the widow to marry the chief immediately
Confiscating all children from the mother
Banning the widow from wearing cloth
explanation: Kuna rites cut the metaphysical ties between living and dead to enable psychic healing and future life.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rites of Passage Q65
stem: What items are traditionally placed inside the coffin or grave with the deceased person?
options: Personal clothing, money, beads, and miniature tools for their onward journey to Asamando
explanation: These grave goods symbolize provisions needed to pay ferry tolls and live honorably in the spiritual world.

stem: What is the primary spiritual significance of traditional festivals in West Africa?
options: To thank God, deities, and ancestors, renew cosmic harmony, settle disputes, and plan community development
To stage theatrical plays for profit
To declare war on neighboring nations
To suspend all farming activities forever
explanation: Festivals serve as sacred moments of religious thanksgiving, social purification, and communal solidarity.

stem: Which historic festival is celebrated by the Ga people of Accra to hoot at hunger?
explanation: Homowo commemorates triumph over a severe ancestral famine experienced during early Ga migration.

stem: What traditional ceremonial food is sprinkled in family houses and shrines during the Homowo festival?
options: Kpokpoi (steamed fermented corn dough eaten with palm nut fish soup)
explanation: Kpokpoi is ceremonially sprinkled by the Ga Mantse and elders to feed spirits and ancestors.

stem: Which festival is celebrated by the Anlo Ewe to commemorate their escape from the tyrannical King Agorkorli at Notsie?
explanation: Hogbetsotso celebrates the dramatic backward walking flight of the Ewes from Notsie in modern Togo.

stem: What symbolic peace-making ceremony precedes the celebration of the Hogbetsotso festival?
options: Dodoleglodi (reconciliation and settlement of all personal and communal grudges)
explanation: Dodoleglodi purifies the community by reconciling all disputes before entering sacred festivities.

stem: Which festival is celebrated by the Efutu people of Winneba featuring the capture of a live bushbuck (deer) with bare hands?
explanation: The two rival Asafo companies (Dentsefo and Tuafo) compete to catch a live deer for the deity Penkye Otu.

stem: What is the annual festival of harvest and cleansing celebrated by the Ahanta and Nzema people of the Western Region?
explanation: Kundum is celebrated across successive towns to mark harvest, drive out evil spirits, and dance with drums.

stem: Which major festival of thanksgiving and purification is celebrated by the Akuapem and Akyem people?
explanation: Odwira purifies the state, mourns ancestors, and celebrates the first harvest of new yams.

stem: Which festival marks the opening of the fishing season and lifting of the fishing ban in Elmina by clearing the Benya Lagoon?
explanation: Bakatue literally means 'the opening of the lagoon' by the Paramount Chief of Elmina.

stem: Which colorful festival is celebrated by the Oguaa (Cape Coast) people in the Central Region?
explanation: Fetu Afahye commemorates deliverance from a historic plague through prayers to the 77 tutelary deities of Cape Coast.

stem: What festival is celebrated in Northern Ghana (Dagbon, Gonja, Mamprusi) to commemorate the birth of the Holy Prophet integrated with royal drumming and horsemanship?
explanation: Damba combines Islamic remembrance with spectacular Northern chieftaincy pomp and horse riding.

stem: What is the Fire Festival celebrated in Dagbon and Mamprugu called?
explanation: Bugum involves carrying burning torches at night to celebrate the historic finding of a lost royal prince.

stem: Which agricultural festival celebrated in Lawra (Upper West Region) features vigorous energetic dancing with waist belts of cowrie shells?
explanation: Kobine is a vibrant post-harvest festival of thanksgiving and athletic dancing in Lawra.

stem: What is the period of complete silence and ban on drumming/noise-making before the Homowo festival called?
explanation: The sacred month of quiet allows the deities to rest and mature the agricultural harvest undisturbed.

stem: How do traditional festivals foster modern socioeconomic development in Ghanaian communities?
options: By attracting homecoming diaspora youth, raising funds for schools/clinics, and boosting local tourism
By closing down all local trade permanently
explanation: Festivals serve as prime avenues for fundraising, communal infrastructure projects, and tourism revenue.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Ethics & Social Control Q81
stem: What are traditional prohibitions and religious bans on certain behaviors called in Akan culture?
explanation: Akyiwadde are sacred prohibitions whose violation causes spiritual pollution and calamity.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Ethics & Social Control Q82
stem: Why was sexual intercourse in the open bush or forest strictly tabooed in traditional society?
options: It defiles the earth goddess (Asaase Yaa) and brings agricultural blight upon the community
It makes people lose their way home
explanation: Adulterating the soil through sexual acts in the bush is an abomination requiring costly animal pacification.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Ethics & Social Control Q83
stem: What is the customary penalty demanded when a person commits an abomination or defiles a sacred taboo?
options: Offering sheep, fowls, eggs, and drinks for purification rituals performed by priests and chiefs
Being sent to study in another country
explanation: Sacrificial blood and libations are required to wipe away spiritual defilement from the community.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Ethics & Social Control Q84
stem: In Akan society, what is the oath sworn by invoking a tragic national disaster or royal wound called?
explanation: Swearing an oath invokes painful ancestral memories to halt actions and force judicial trial.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Ethics & Social Control Q85
stem: What is the sacred purpose of swearing the Great Oath (Ntam Kese) in traditional jurisprudence?
options: To halt an injustice, transfer a dispute immediately before the King's court, and establish sacred truth
To insult one's neighbors in public
explanation: Swearing an oath freezes the situation and brings both parties before the supreme royal court.

stem: What is the traditional Akan concept of human nature comprised of (Okra, Sunsum, Mogya, Ntoro)?
options: Okra (soul), Sunsum (personality), Mogya (blood from mother), Ntoro (spirit from father)
explanation: Akan philosophical anthropology combines divine soul, father's spirit, and mother's bloodline.

stem: Which component of human personality is received directly from Onyankopon as the divine spark of life?
explanation: The Okra is the immortal divine breath given by God carrying an individual's destiny (Nkrabea).

stem: In matrilineal inheritance (such as the Akan), what determines a person's clan (Abusua) membership?
options: The village where one is born
explanation: Clanship is transmitted matrilineally through maternal blood, governing inheritance and succession.

stem: What is the sacred paternal spirit that shapes a person's character, temperament, and moral fortitude called?
explanation: The father transmits the Ntoro / Sunsum which determines spiritual resilience, taboos, and protection.

stem: What is the rule forbidding marriage between members of the same ancestral clan called?
options: Exogamy (prohibition of clan incest / incest taboo)
explanation: Members of the same Abusua are deemed spiritual brothers and sisters; marriage between them is taboo.

stem: How does traditional religion contribute to environmental conservation in modern Ghana?
options: By preserving sacred groves, declaring river fishing taboos, and protecting endangered animal totems
By cutting down all virgin rainforests
By encouraging industrial waste disposal in rivers
explanation: Sacred groves (e.g., monkey sanctuaries) and river taboos preserve precious biodiversity from exploitation.

stem: What is a totem (Akyeneboa) in indigenous clan organization?
options: A sacred animal, bird, or plant adopted as a clan symbol and protected from hunting or harm
A stone weight used to weigh gold
explanation: Totems remind clan members of historic ancestral alliances with nature and instill ecological reverence.

stem: Which of the following values is regarded as the cornerstone of traditional communal life?
options: Solidarity, mutual cooperation, hospitality, respect for elders, and honesty
explanation: Indigenous ethics prioritize harmonious community life: 'I am because we are, and since we are, therefore I am.'

stem: How does traditional religion view honesty and truthfulness in judicial testimonies?
options: Lying under oath invites swift divine retribution, madness, or spiritual death from the ancestors
Lying is acceptable if one makes money
Ancestors do not care about truth
explanation: The unseen spirit world guarantees justice; lying under sacred oaths invokes ancestral vengeance.

stem: What enduring role does traditional religion continue to play in contemporary modern Ghana?
options: Providing moral identity, preserving indigenous cultural heritage, chieftaincy legitimacy, and conflict resolution
explanation: Traditional values enrich national identity, cultural pride, alternative dispute resolution, and ecological ethics.

stem: What are the ornate military post shrines constructed by Fante Asafo companies called?
explanation: Posuban shrines serve as elaborate civic monuments and storage posts for Asafo regalia and totems.

stem: Which dark mourning cloths are customarily worn by Akan mourners during deep bereavement and funerals?
explanation: Dark brown, red (kobene), and black cloths symbolize intense sorrow, blood, and loss.

stem: What pedagogical purpose do traditional Akan spider folktales (Anansesem) serve in community life?
options: Inculcating moral wisdom, virtues, and warning children against greed and cunning
explanation: Anansesem uses humorous animal allegories to teach social morality, honesty, and common sense.

stem: Why is the use of the left hand strictly tabooed when greeting elders, gesturing, or presenting gifts in Ghanaian culture?
options: The left hand is regarded as unclean and disrespectful in social interaction
The left hand is weaker than the right
The left hand is reserved for writing only
It breaks the chief's walking stick
explanation: Presenting items or waving with the left hand is an insult; the right hand is required for civil etiquette.

stem: What unique role do the Akan talking drums (Atumpan) play in royal courts and festivals?
options: Broadcasting drum poetry, praising kings, and reciting ancestral epithets and proverbs
Keeping time for modern factory workers
Replacing human speech entirely in conversation
explanation: Atumpan mimic the tonal inflections of the Akan language to communicate historical and sacred praise.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q1
stem: How many lines and spaces make up the standard modern musical staff (stave)?
explanation: A musical staff consists of five parallel horizontal lines and four intervening spaces.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q2
stem: Which musical clef is also designated as the 'G clef' because its spiral curls around the second line?
explanation: The treble clef establishes the pitch G above middle C on the second line.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q3
stem: Which clef is known as the 'F clef' because its two dots surround the fourth line of the staff?
explanation: The bass clef places the note F below middle C on the fourth line.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q4
stem: What is the note value of a semibreve in common time (4/4)?
explanation: A semibreve (whole note) has a duration value of four crotchet beats.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q5
stem: How many quavers (eighth notes) are equivalent in total duration to one minim (half note)?
explanation: A minim equals two crotchets, and each crotchet equals two quavers (2 x 2 = 4).

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q6
stem: What effect does placing a dot immediately after a note head produce?
options: It increases the duration of the note by half of its original value
It lowers the pitch by a semitone
It raises the pitch by an octave
explanation: A dotted minim, for instance, gets 2 + 1 = 3 beats.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q7
stem: What is the pitch value of the note situated on the middle ledger line between the treble and bass staves?
explanation: Middle C sits on a ledger line directly between the bass and treble staves.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q8
stem: What accidental symbol raises the pitch of a note by one semitone (half step)?
explanation: A sharp raises pitch by a semitone, whereas a flat lowers it by a semitone.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q9
stem: What accidental symbol cancels a previous sharp or flat and restores the note to its normal pitch?
explanation: The natural sign cancels any previous accidental within that bar.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Rudiments of Music Q10
stem: What do two notes that have different pitch names but sound at the identical acoustic pitch called (e.g., C# and Db)?
explanation: Enharmonic notes share identical sounding pitch despite distinct musical notation.

stem: What is the semitone pattern of intervals that defines every Major scale ascending from tonic to tonic?
options: Tone - Tone - Semitone - Tone - Tone - Tone - Semitone
Tone - Semitone - Tone - Tone - Semitone - Tone - Tone
Semitone - Tone - Tone - Semitone - Tone - Tone - Tone
Tone - Tone - Tone - Tone - Semitone - Semitone - Tone
explanation: T-T-S-T-T-T-S is the universal diatonic formula for a major scale.

stem: How many sharps are found in the key signature of G Major?
explanation: G major has one sharp on F.

stem: Which major key has three flats (Bb, Eb, Ab) in its key signature?
explanation: E-flat major contains Bb, Eb, and Ab in its key signature.

stem: What is the relative minor key to C Major having no sharps and no flats?
explanation: A minor is the relative minor of C major, sharing identical key signatures.

stem: In a Harmonic Minor scale, which scale degree is raised by one semitone both ascending and descending?
explanation: The harmonic minor raises the 7th degree to create a leading tone semitone to the tonic.

stem: What is the technical sol-fa name given to the fifth degree of any diatonic scale?
explanation: Scale degrees: 1=Tonic, 2=Supertonic, 3=Mediant, 4=Subdominant, 5=Dominant, 6=Submediant, 7=Leading tone.

stem: What is the distance in pitch between any two musical notes called?
explanation: An interval measures the pitch distance between two sounding notes.

stem: What is the interval between C and G called?
explanation: C to G encompasses 5 letter names and 7 semitones, forming a Perfect 5th.

stem: When an interval is larger than an octave (such as a 9th or 11th), it is termed a:
explanation: Intervals exceeding an octave are classified as compound intervals.

stem: A standard musical triad consists of which three harmonic scale degrees?
explanation: A triad is formed by stacking two thirds above a fundamental root note.

stem: What type of triad is formed with a root, a minor third, and a diminished fifth?
explanation: A diminished triad contains two consecutive minor thirds.

stem: In musical harmony, what is a musical punctuation mark that concludes a phrase or piece called?
explanation: A cadence is a harmonic progression that concludes a phrase.

stem: Which cadence moves from the Dominant chord (V) to the Tonic chord (I), producing a feeling of complete finality?
explanation: A V-I progression with tonic in soprano and bass creates a conclusive Perfect cadence.

stem: Which cadence is commonly known as the 'Amen' cadence and moves from the Subdominant (IV) to the Tonic (I)?
explanation: The IV-I progression is widely used for choir 'Amens' in church liturgy.

stem: What is an Imperfect cadence (half cadence)?
options: A progression ending on the Dominant chord (such as I-V, II-V, or IV-V)
A progression from V to VI
A progression from I to IV
A progression from V to I
explanation: An imperfect cadence ends on V, sounding unfinished and expecting continuation.

stem: What is the top number in a simple time signature (such as 3/4) indicating?
options: The number of beats contained in each measure (bar)
The kind of note receiving one beat
The pitch of the first note
explanation: The numerator denotes the number of beats per measure.

stem: What does the bottom number '8' in a compound time signature like 6/8 represent?
explanation: The denominator '8' indicates eighth notes (quavers).

stem: In 6/8 time signature, how many dotted crotchet main beats are there per bar?
options: Two main dotted crotchet beats (compound duple)
explanation: 6/8 is compound duple meter with two main beats of three quavers each.

stem: What dynamic Italian term directs the performer to play very softly?
explanation: Pianissimo indicates very soft volume; piano indicates soft.

stem: What Italian tempo marking signifies a fast, lively, and brisk speed?
explanation: Allegro means cheerful, fast, and lively.

stem: What does the Italian term 'Crescendo' (cresc.) instruct the musician to do?
explanation: Crescendo indicates a gradual increase in sound volume.

stem: What musical term indicates singing without any instrumental accompaniment?
explanation: A cappella singing is purely vocal choral performance without instruments.

stem: What does the symbol of a curved line connecting two notes of the same pitch indicate?
options: A Tie (combining their durations into one unbroken sound)
explanation: A tie binds identical pitches together into an extended single note duration.

stem: What musical articulation mark instructs a performer to play notes short, crisp, and detached?
explanation: Staccato (indicated by a dot over/under the note head) means detached and brief.

stem: What is the pause or hold symbol placed over a note or rest called?
explanation: A fermata prolongs a note beyond its strict metrical duration at the conductor's discretion.

stem: In the Hornbostel-Sachs classification of musical instruments, what is an 'Idiophone'?
options: An instrument whose sound is produced by the vibration of its own solid resonant body
An instrument sounding by a vibrating stretched skin
An instrument sounding by vibrating air columns
explanation: Idiophones (bells, rattles, slit drums, xylophones) vibrate their own substance.

stem: Which of the following Ghanaian instruments is classified as an idiophone?
explanation: The dawuru is a clapperless iron bell struck with a stick, classified as a struck idiophone.

stem: What is a 'Membranophone' in African organology?
options: An instrument that produces sound primarily through the vibration of a tightly stretched skin or membrane
A brass horn blown by lips
A stringed lute played with fingers
explanation: Membranophones include all single- and double-headed drums covered with animal hide.

stem: What is the famous Akan talking drum pair consisting of a male and female drum called?
explanation: The Atumpan pair is tuned to low and high tones to emulate speech inflections.

stem: Which Ghanaian hourglass-shaped squeeze drum is held under the armpit and changes pitch when cords are squeezed?
explanation: The donno varies pitch continuously by compressing the longitudinal leather thongs.

stem: What is the paramount, grand state ensemble of massive drums used for royal Akan kings called?
explanation: Fontomfrom is the majestic royal court orchestra for paramount chiefs and state durbars.

stem: Which court dance and drum ensemble was historically introduced into the Ashanti court from the Gyaman Kingdom?
explanation: Kete is an elegant royal court music with distinctive black-and-red checked drum cloths.

stem: Which graceful Akan recreational and funeral dance ensemble uses drums called Apentemma, Petia, and Atumpan?
explanation: Adowa is the quintessential Akan communal dance celebrated for delicate hand and foot gestures.

stem: Which vibrant traditional musical and dance style is celebrated by the Ewe people featuring the Sogo and Kidi drums?
explanation: Agbadza evolved from ancient Ewe war dances (Atrikpui) into a joyful communal dance.

stem: In Ewe master drumming, what is the role of the large lead drum known as the 'Atsimevu'?
options: It directs the ensemble, gives signals, and improvises complex rhythmic variations
It only plays a steady monotonous pulse
It remains completely silent during dances
It is only played by young children
explanation: The Atsimevu is the master drum commanding all choreography and rhythmic changes.

stem: What is the high-pitched wooden bell or iron clapper that plays the recurring timeline (ostinato) in Ewe drumming?
explanation: The Gankogui provides the fundamental unvarying metric anchor (timeline) for the entire ensemble.

stem: What gourd rattle netted with beads or seeds is played in Ewe and Ga ensembles?
explanation: The Axatse is a dried calabash covered with a bead net struck against hand and thigh.

stem: What recreational youth dance music emerged in Accra among the Ga people in the late 1950s using conga-like drums?
explanation: Kpanlogo was developed by Ga youth in post-independence Accra with infectious dance rhythms.

stem: Which instrument played extensively in Northern Ghana (Dagaaba, Birifor, Lobi) is a wooden xylophone with calabash resonators?
explanation: The Gyil features wooden bars suspended over dried gourd resonators fitted with mirliton membranes.

stem: What single-string bowed fiddle played in Dagbon and northern savannah regions is called:
explanation: The Goje is a bowed chordophone with a horsehair string played by royal griots and praise-singers.

stem: What is the traditional Akan harp-lute with wooden box resonator and strings called?
explanation: The Seprewa is an authentic Akan chordophone preceding the acoustic guitar.

stem: Which category of instruments produce sound by vibrating air columns, including flutes and horns?
explanation: Aerophones encompass all wind instruments such as bamboo flutes and ivory tusks (asento).

stem: What are the royal animal horns or elephant tusk flutes blown by court musicians called in Akan courts?
options: Asento (or Mmensoun - ensemble of seven ivory horns)
explanation: Mmensoun consists of seven ivory horns that blow surrogate poetic phrases for the paramount chief.

stem: Which post-harvest energetic social dance is performed by the Dagomba people featuring men dressed in flared skirts (kurugu)?
explanation: Bamaya is a comic and energetic Dagomba dance where men twist their waists in ruffled skirts.

stem: What harvest and recreational dance is performed by the Dagaaba and Sissala people of Upper West Ghana?
explanation: Bawa is the athletic communal harvest dance of the Dagaaba people.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q56
stem: What is the prevailing structural vocal texture in traditional African choral singing?
explanation: Call-and-response alternates between a soloist leader and a choral answering refrain.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q57
stem: What rhythmic phenomenon occurs when two or more conflicting rhythmic patterns (such as 3 against 2) sound simultaneously?
explanation: Polyrhythm is the layering of independent rhythmic meters over a shared underlying pulse.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q58
stem: What is a short, persistently repeated rhythmic or melodic phrase throughout an African piece called?
explanation: The ostinato timeline (often played on an iron bell) provides the temporal reference point.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q59
stem: In what tuning system do many traditional African xylophone and vocal traditions organize their scales?
explanation: Equi-heptatonic (seven equidistant steps) and pentatonic (five-note) scales are prevalent across Ghana.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q60
stem: How is traditional musical knowledge and drumming skill primarily transmitted across generations in Africa?
options: Oral tradition, observation, imitation, and active communal participation
Reading printed sheet music in schools
explanation: Musicianship is absorbed orally from childhood through family guilds and cultural immersion.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q61
stem: What is the term for speech surrogacy where drums emulate the linguistic tones, stresses, and phrases of tonal language?
explanation: Because languages like Akan and Ewe are tonal, drums can articulate intelligible proverbs.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q62
stem: In traditional Ghanaian worldview, can music and dance be totally separated from daily social events?
options: No, music is integrated into ceremonies, rites of passage, labor, worship, and social recreation
Yes, music is only performed in silent closed auditoriums
No, music is completely prohibited in public
Yes, music only exists for commercial sale
explanation: African music is functional and interwoven with every dimension of human life.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q63
stem: What is the social role of the traditional master drummer (Okyerema)?
options: He is the historian, poet, musician, and custodian of oral traditions in the royal court
He serves as the chief judge in high court
explanation: The Okyerema holds a sacred office preserving royal history and community lore through his drums.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q64
stem: Why is clapping an essential element of African musical performance?
options: It allows the entire audience to participate actively and reinforce the rhythmic timeline
It signals the end of the day
It serves as a punishment for bad dancing
explanation: Active clapping engages the community, transforming passive spectators into active co-creators.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - African Music Characteristics Q65
stem: What is the metric shift where accentuation falls off the normal strong beat onto a weak beat?
explanation: Syncopation imparts rhythmic drive and vitality by accenting normally unaccented beats.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Western Music History Q66
stem: Which period of Western music history spanned approximately 1600 to 1750 and featured ornate counterpoint and basso continuo?
explanation: The Baroque era (1600-1750) was exemplified by Bach, Handel, and Vivaldi.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Western Music History Q67
stem: Which German Baroque master composed the 'Brandenburg Concertos' and 'The Well-Tempered Clavier'?
explanation: J.S. Bach (1685-1750) is universally revered as the supreme master of Baroque counterpoint.

syllabusRef: WAEC Syllabus - Western Music History Q68
